title: Three Famous Food Markets in Europe
summary: Visit three famous food markets in Barcelona, Paris and London. Meet the farmers, neighbours, cooks and traders who shaped them, discover what people eat there today, then use practical English to buy food, check ingredients, pay and tip.

cover.alt: An adult traveller explores a collage of produce, cheese and street-food markets in Barcelona, Paris and London.

blocks.title: Three Markets, Three Shopping Trips
paragraphs: Visit three famous food markets in Barcelona, Paris and London. Meet the farmers, neighbours, cooks and traders who shaped them, discover what people eat there today, then use practical English to buy food, check ingredients, pay and tip.

items.prompt: What food do you like to buy at a market?
items.explanation: You can name fruit, bread, cheese, a snack or another food.

items.prompt: Which city would you like to visit: Barcelona, Paris or London?
items.explanation: Choose one city and give one simple reason.

items.explanation: Think about the price, ingredients, amount or payment.

blocks.title: La Boqueria: Colour and Choice in Barcelona
paragraphs: La Boqueria stands on La Rambla, but its story began before the covered market. In 1217, records described meat stalls there. Many early sellers were farmers from villages around Barcelona, bringing food into the city. Traders moved to the present site in 1836. Today, more than 200 traders open their shutters. Visitors pass bright fruit and vegetables, olives and preserved foods, meat, fish and seafood. Small bars serve food beside the shopping stalls. The market still connects two groups: people who sell food and people who come to shop, eat and talk. It has a long history, but it is also part of everyday city life.

items.prompt: How did La Boqueria first connect villages around Barcelona with the city?
items.answer: Farmers from nearby villages brought food to La Rambla and sold it from market stalls.
items.explanation: The market grew from a place where farmers and city shoppers met.

rows.meaning: Ask the seller for a popular choice.
Ask whether the food comes from the area.
Order a small amount of food by weight.
Ask whether card payment is possible.

blocks.title: Marché des Enfants Rouges: Old Paris, Many Flavours
paragraphs: Marché des Enfants Rouges is Paris's oldest covered food market. Its unusual name means “Market of the Red Children.” It remembers children from a nearby home who wore red clothes. In the 1990s, there was a plan to replace the old market with a car park. Traders and neighbours protested and even slept outside to save it. Today, their market is full of different people and foods. Tom's team serves Moroccan chicken skewers and couscous. Julienne cooks Creole food with flavours from Cameroon. Visitors can also buy farm cheese, Breton buckwheat galettes, oysters, fresh fruit juice, and organic fruit and vegetables.

items.prompt: How did traders and neighbours help Marché des Enfants Rouges survive?
items.answer: They protested and even slept outside when there was a plan to replace the market with a car park.
items.explanation: Their action saved the market, so traders and cooks can still work there today.

rows.meaning: Ask whether nuts are an ingredient.

blocks.title: Borough Market: Produce and Street Food in London
paragraphs: Borough Market's story goes back about 1,000 years, when people sold food near London Bridge. In 1756, local parishioners moved it to the place where it stands today. The market is now a charity. Volunteer trustees run it for shoppers, traders and neighbours, so it is still a community place, not only a tourist sight. More than 100 businesses sell food there. Applebee's offers British seafood, Arabica serves Middle Eastern meze, falafel and shawarma, and Bao Borough makes bao buns. Visitors can shop for cheese and other ingredients, choose a hot lunch, and meet some of the people who feed London today.

items.prompt: Why is Borough Market more than only a tourist sight?
items.answer: It is a working food market and a charity run for shoppers, traders, neighbours and the wider community.
items.explanation: Local people shaped its history, and more than 100 food businesses work there today.

blocks.title: Tipping in Spain, France and the UK
paragraphs: Tipping customs change between Spain, France and the UK. At a simple market stall or self-service counter, people normally pay the displayed price unless the seller says otherwise. In Spain, a tip is optional, and some people simply round up the bill. In France, restaurant prices normally include service, so extra money is optional. In the UK, a restaurant bill may include a discretionary or compulsory service charge. A visitor should read the bill before adding more money. The rules can feel different, but you do not need to guess. The safest habit in all three countries is simple: check the bill, then ask.

items.prompt: What should a visitor do before adding money for service?
items.answer: Read the bill first, then ask if the situation is still unclear.
items.explanation: Tipping customs differ, and a restaurant bill may already include service.

rows.meaning: Ask whether service is already in the price.
Ask whether money for service is on the bill.

rows.term: Do I need to leave a tip?
rows.meaning: Ask whether an extra tip is expected.
rows.example: Do I need to leave a tip?

blocks.title: Scene 1: Buy Olives and Fruit at La Boqueria
paragraphs: You are at an olive-and-fruit counter inside La Boqueria on La Rambla. Colourful produce and specialist food counters fill the market. Olives are sold by weight, and baskets of peaches stand nearby. You can ask, “What is popular here?” and “Is this local?” You hear one shopper say, “Two hundred grams, please.” Another shopper asks, “Do you take cards?”
Your goal is to choose local food, buy 200 grams of olives and two peaches, check card payment, and complete the purchase.

images.alt: An adult traveller talks with a seller weighing olives beside two peaches and a card terminal at a covered Barcelona market stall.

turns.speaker: Seller
turns.text: Hello. What can I get you?

turns.speaker: Seller
turns.text: These green olives are very popular.

turns.speaker: Seller
turns.text: Yes, these olives are from Catalonia.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Great. Two hundred grams, please, and two peaches.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: No, thank you. Do you take cards?

blocks.title: Scene 2: Check Ingredients in Paris
paragraphs: You are at a prepared-food counter inside Marché des Enfants Rouges, Paris's oldest covered food market. Around you, cooks serve dishes from several cultures. A rice-and-vegetable dish looks good, but you have a nut allergy. First ask, “What is in this?” Then ask, “Does this contain nuts?” and say, “I am allergic to nuts.” If the dish is unsafe, point to a sealed bottle of water and say, “One of these, please.”
Your goal is to check the dish, explain your allergy, refuse food that is not safe for you, and order a drink instead.

images.alt: An adult traveller checks an illustrated ingredient card with a cook beside a prepared dish and sealed water at a covered Paris market.

blocks.title: Roleplay 2: Ask About a Nut Allergy

turns.speaker: Cook
turns.text: Hello. Would you like this rice-and-vegetable dish?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: It looks good. What is in this?

turns.speaker: Cook
turns.text: It has rice, vegetables and a sauce.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Does this contain nuts? I am allergic to nuts.

turns.speaker: Cook
turns.text: Yes. The sauce contains almonds, and other food here may also touch nuts.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Thank you for telling me. I won't have the dish.

turns.speaker: Cook
turns.text: Of course. Would you like a drink?

blocks.title: Scene 3: Buy Lunch at Borough Market
paragraphs: You are at a street-food counter in Borough Market Kitchen. It is one of the market's three main areas, and the wider market has more than 100 food businesses. A worker is making hot cheese toasties while customers pay. One visitor asks, “Is service included?” You want to ask, “Is there a service charge?” and “Do I need to leave a tip?”
Your goal is to order one toastie, pay by card, ask about the service charge and tip, and complete the payment.

images.alt: An adult traveller holds a bank card beside a terminal while a market worker serves one cheese toastie under London market arches.

turns.speaker: Counter Worker
turns.text: No. The price is seven pounds.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Do I need to leave a tip?
